subject: Cooking
title: How Yeast Makes Alcohol
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on How Yeast Makes Alcohol.

hook.text: Yeast eats sugar and produces alcohol and CO2. Humanity's favorite beverages are yeast's waste products.

buildup.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae — brewer's yeast — has been humanity's fermentation partner for 9,000 years.

discovery.text: One glucose molecule yields two ethanol molecules and two CO2 molecules. Simple chemistry, complex flavors.

twist.text: Yeast dies when alcohol exceeds 15–18%. That's why most wines and beers stay below that threshold.

climax.text: Distilled spirits bypass this limit by concentrating alcohol through evaporation and condensation.

punchline.text: Every glass of wine is a graveyard of yeast that drowned in its own creation.

quiz.question: Why do most wines have less than 18% alcohol?

details.summary: Yeast converts sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide through anaerobic respiration. Different yeast strains produce different alcohol levels, flavors, and aromas. This single biological process is responsible for all beer, wine, spirits, and naturally leavened bread.
details.whyItMatters: Alcoholic fermentation is one of humanity's oldest biotechnologies. Understanding yeast metabolism explains why different beverages taste so different despite using the same basic process.
takeaways: Yeast converts one glucose molecule into two ethanol and two CO2
Different yeast strains create distinct flavors and aromas
Temperature and sugar concentration control fermentation speed

faq.question: Why does yeast stop producing alcohol at certain levels?
faq.answer: Ethanol is toxic to yeast cells. Most strains die around 14 to 18 percent alcohol concentration. Wine yeast tolerates higher levels than beer yeast. Spirits achieve higher alcohol through distillation after fermentation, not through yeast alone.

faq.question: What determines the flavor of fermented beverages?
faq.answer: Yeast strain, temperature, sugar source, and fermentation time all contribute. Esters create fruity aromas, phenols add spicy notes, and fusel alcohols contribute warmth. Winemakers and brewers select specific strains and conditions to craft desired flavor profiles.
